No free lunch: The perils of two-timepoint change in non-randomized designs

Residualized Change vs. Change Scores in the presence of measurement error

Author
Affiliation

Nicholas Judd

Stockholm University

Published

June 1, 2026

Theoretical Background

To measure human behavior we use tasks or questionnaires in an attempt to measure hypothesized underlying latent constructs (e.g., cognitive ability, personality, or psychiatric disorders). This makes it near impossible to measure human behavior without error - any observed score is a noisy proxy of the underlying true value — contaminated by factors such as task/measurement reliability, participant state, and sampling variability (for a full theoretical account of error see van Bork et al., 2024).

Measurement error (ε) is the rule, not the exception. This makes it very difficult to measure the change in a construct over time, as our first measurement (T1) does not represent fully measure ability at that point of time; it is simply a proxy, and the degree to which it tracks the true latent construct depends on the reliability of the measure.

\[\text{Latent Construct Y} = T_1 + \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]

I am not the first to highlight that residual change analysis leads to consistent and strong false positives, yet despite numerous papers highlighting this issue, the method remains prevalent in empirical articles without randomized designs (for a brief selection see: van Breukelen, 2006; Castro Schilo & Grimm, 2018; Tennant et al., 2023).

This document demonstrates how residualized change also known as ANCOVA of change (regressing T2 on X while covarying T1) and change scores (T2 − T1) behave differently in non-randomized contexts.

The key point: these two measures differ with their relationship to an IV (X) - with residualized change analysis the outcome is Y at T2, not on change itself — this distinction matters when baseline ability (T1) is measured with noise.

The change score approach first computes a difference score and then regresses it on the predictor:

\[\Delta\text{Y} = T_2 - T_1\]

\[\Delta\text{Y} \sim X\]

The residualized change approach instead regresses T2 directly on X while statistically controlling for T1:

\[T_2 \sim X + T_1\] According the the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem if we residualize T2 for T1 and also residualize X for T1 it is equal to the above equation.

\[T_{2_{res}} \sim X_{res}\]

See my post on how if you only residualize your outcome (Y) it will 1) change the relationship of X on Y and 2) mess with the size of your standardized effects. Moreover (Δ ~ T1 == T2 ~ T1), see Castro Schilo & Grimm, 2018 or see my code gist.

This is not a full treatment of how the T1–T2 correlation modulates residualized change estimates; it simply illustrates the basic mechanics. For a great post on how residualized change adds power in RCT designs see this blog post.

Code 
rm(list = ls())
if (!require(pacman)) install.packages("pacman")
options(scipen = 999)
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, data.table, MASS, QuantPsyc, modelsummary, tinytable, patchwork)
Code 
n      <- 1000
n_reps <- 1000
r <- 0.4  # baseline correlation: ability ~ skill use
d <- 0    # no true relationship between X and change

set.seed(33)
s <- matrix(c(1, r, 0,
              r, 1, d,
              0, d, 1), nrow = 3)
# rows/cols: 1 = T1, 2 = X (skill use), 3 = delta (change)

These two approaches are highly related & usually correlated, what matters is the how the variance that is left is related to an IV (X)

Code 
r_prev <- round(cor(tb_prev$sub_delta, tb_prev$resid_change), 2)

ggplot(tb_prev, aes(x = sub_delta, y = resid_change)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#2166ac", fill = "#2166ac") +
  annotate("text", x = Inf, y = -Inf, hjust = 1.1, vjust = -0.8,
           label = paste0("r = ", r_prev), size = 4.5) +
  labs(title = "Correlation of both approaches", subtitle = "False positive's are with the relationship to a IV (X)",
       x = "ΔY (T2 − T1)\n with measurement noise",
       y = "Residualized change (T2_res)\n with measurement noise") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

Simulation description

Here we are interested in the relationship of an IV (X) with change in Y overtime (ΔY). In Case 1 we simulate without measurement error and in Case 2 we add measurement error.

The following conditions hold:

  1. A baseline relationship between X and Y (this is the cross-sectional association and not the estimand of interest)
  2. We simulate a case where X does not predict longitudinal change in Y (Δ = 0)
  3. \(Y_{T2} = Y_{T1} + ΔY\)
Code 
as.data.frame(s) |>
  setNames(c("T1", "X", "Δ")) |>
  mutate(var1 = c("T1", "X", "Δ")) |>
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "r") |>
  mutate(var1 = factor(var1, levels = c("Δ", "X", "T1")),
         var2 = factor(var2, levels = c("T1", "X", "Δ"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = var2, y = var1, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(r, 2)), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#d73027", mid = "white", high = "#2166ac",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "r",
       title = "Population correlation matrix") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

We draw n = 1000 observations from a multivariate normal distribution with three variables:

  • baseline ability in Y (T1),
  • a predictor of interest (X, representing skill use),
  • and true change in Y (ΔY)

To reflect a baseline relationship, T1 and X are correlated positively (r = 0.4) — those with higher ability in Y at T1 also tend to show higher skill use (X). Critically, Δ is uncorrelated with both T1 and X: nothing is actually happening over time, so any apparent effect of X on change must be spurious due to the baseline relationship (T1 ~ X).

The follow-up score T2 is simply the sum of baseline ability (T1 without measurement error) and true change:

\[T_2 = T_1 + \Delta\]

This means the only source of genuine longitudinal signal in T2 is Δ, which is independent of X. Any model that recovers a non-zero effect of X on T2 (or on change) is therefore producing a false positive.

Later on, in Case 2 we illustrate the effect of measurement error by adding random Gaussian noise to Y at T1 to get two imperfect measures of baseline ability. Increasing \(\sigma^2\) values increase the proportion of measurement noise.

\[T1_{m1} = T_1 + \varepsilon_1, \quad \varepsilon_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]

\[T1_{m2} = T_1 + \varepsilon_2, \quad \varepsilon_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]

Case 1: \(Y_{T1}\) perfectly measured (no measurement error)

When T1 is measured without error, change scores and residualized change give the same (correct) answer:

No effect of X on change Illustrated by the lack of significance of X on the model table below.

Code 
set.seed(30)
dat2 <- as.data.frame(mvrnorm(n, mu = c(0, 0, 0), Sigma = s))
colnames(dat2) <- c("T1", "X", "delta")
dat2$T2        <- dat2$T1 + dat2$delta
dat2$sub_delta <- dat2$T2 - dat2$T1

m_perfect <- list(
  "Change score" = lm(sub_delta ~ X,  data = dat2),
  "Residualized" = lm(T2 ~ X + T1,   data = dat2)
)

sig_rows <- {
  df <- modelsummary(m_perfect, statistic = NULL, stars = TRUE, output = "dataframe")
  which(df[["term"]] == "X" & apply(df[, -(1:2), drop = FALSE], 1, function(x) any(grepl("\\*", x))))
}

modelsummary(m_perfect,
  statistic = NULL,
  stars     = TRUE,
  gof_map   = c("nobs", "r.squared", "adj.r.squared")
) |>
  style_tt(i = sig_rows, bold = TRUE)
Change score Residualized
+ p < 0.1, * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001
(Intercept) 0.014 0.014
X 0.042 0.050
T1 0.982***
Num.Obs. 1000 1000
R2 0.002 0.507
R2 Adj. 0.001 0.506

Both models recover the null effect (β ≈ 0) because T1 is perfectly captured. The intercept-only variance in T2 after removing T1 is purely delta, which is uncorrelated with X by design.

Case 2: Allowing measurment error (adding noise to T1)

In practice, baseline scores are measured with error. Here we add gaussian noise (\(\sigma^2\) = 0.7) to create two imperfect measurements of T1.

  • T1_measure1 — the baseline measurement used as a predictor

\[T1_{m1} = T_1 + \varepsilon_1, \quad \varepsilon_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]

  • T1_measure2 — a second measurement used to construct T2

\[T1_{m2} = T_1 + \varepsilon_2, \quad \varepsilon_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]

Note, both of these reflect an imperfect measure of Y. \(T1_{m2}\) is not simulating test–retest noise by adding noise to \(T1_{m1}\) - rather both reflect the reality that we cannot perfectly measure the latent construct Y at T1. For our T1 measure we now use \(T1_{m1}\) and our followup score (T2) with T1 measurement error becomes the following:

\[T_{2_{m2}} = T_{1_{m2}} + \Delta\text{Y}\]

Code 
setDT(dat2)
true_base <- dat2[, .(T1, X, delta)]

sd_val <- 0.7

set.seed(892)
true_base$T1_measure1 <- true_base$T1 + rnorm(nrow(true_base), 0, sd_val)
set.seed(12)
true_base$T1_measure2 <- true_base$T1 + rnorm(nrow(true_base), 0, sd_val)

To clarify, the second time we measure Y at T2, this variable is the amount of change in Y between the two time points (ΔY) plus ability level at T1 imperfectly measured again (\(T1_{m2}\)). In practice, ΔY is also measured with error yet as we are simulating the null (ΔY = 0) and it is not needed for this example we will ignore it for now.

This makes our delta equation the following:

\[\Delta\text{Y}_{m} = T_{2_{m2}} - T_{1_{m1}}\] Our change equation now looks like this: \[\Delta\text{Y}_{m} \sim X\]

The residualized change equations looks like this: \[T_{2_{m2}} \sim X + T_{1_{m1}}\]

Writing these equations out hopefully clarifies the role of measurement error, and makes explicit the issues of residual confounding. In this toy example these two noisy measures of Y at T1 correlate: 0.7, below in Case 3 we will vary the amount of noise.

Code 
true_base$T2        <- true_base$T1_measure2 + true_base$delta
true_base$sub_delta <- true_base$T2 - true_base$T1_measure1

m_noisy <- list(
  "Change score"      = lm(sub_delta ~ X,        data = true_base),
  "Resid. (noisy T1)" = lm(T2 ~ X + T1_measure1, data = true_base),
  "Resid. (true T1)"  = lm(T2 ~ X + T1,          data = true_base)
)

sig_rows <- {
  df <- modelsummary(m_noisy, statistic = NULL, stars = TRUE, output = "dataframe")
  which(df[["term"]] == "X" & apply(df[, -(1:2), drop = FALSE], 1, function(x) any(grepl("\\*", x))))
}

modelsummary(m_noisy,
  statistic   = NULL,
  stars       = TRUE,
  gof_map     = c("nobs", "r.squared", "adj.r.squared"),
  coef_rename = c("T1_measure1" = "T1 (noisy)", "T1" = "T1 (true)")
) |>
  style_tt(i = sig_rows, bold = TRUE)
Change score Resid. (noisy T1) Resid. (true T1)
+ p < 0.1, * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001
(Intercept) 0.035 0.011 -0.004
X 0.003 0.178*** 0.032
T1 (noisy) 0.647***
T1 (true) 1.008***
Num.Obs. 1000 1000 1000
R2 0.000 0.322 0.431
R2 Adj. -0.001 0.321 0.429

The residualized change model with the noisy T1 measure now shows a spurious positive effect of X. Because T1_measure1 doesn’t fully partial out true Y at T1, and X is correlated with true Y at T1, the coefficient for X absorbs that residual variance.

Code 
tb <- as.data.frame(true_base)
tb$resid_change <- resid(lm(T2 ~ T1_measure1, data = tb))

bind_rows(
  data.frame(X = tb$X, y = tb$sub_delta,     approach = "Change score  (Δ ~ X)"),
  data.frame(X = tb$X, y = tb$resid_change,  approach = "Residualized change (T2 ~ X + T1)")
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = X, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#d73027", fill = "#d73027") +
  facet_wrap(~approach, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "X (skill use)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

Lets make sure this holds by replicating it a 1000 times

Code 
set.seed(2027)
pval_sd <- 0.7

pval_reps <- replicate(n_reps, {
  sim <- as.data.frame(mvrnorm(n, mu = c(0, 0, 0), Sigma = s))
  colnames(sim) <- c("T1", "X", "delta")
  sim$T1_m1  <- sim$T1 + rnorm(n, 0, pval_sd)
  sim$T1_m2  <- sim$T1 + rnorm(n, 0, pval_sd)
  sim$T2     <- sim$T1_m2 + sim$delta
  sim$change <- sim$T2 - sim$T1_m1
  m_cs <- lm(change ~ X,      data = sim)
  m_rn <- lm(T2 ~ X + T1_m1, data = sim)
  m_rt <- lm(T2 ~ X + T1,    data = sim)
  c(
    pval_change_score = summary(m_cs)$coefficients["X", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    pval_resid_noisy  = summary(m_rn)$coefficients["X", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    pval_resid_true   = summary(m_rt)$coefficients["X", "Pr(>|t|)"]
  )
})

pval_df <- data.frame(
  p     = c(pval_reps["pval_change_score", ],
            pval_reps["pval_resid_noisy",  ],
            pval_reps["pval_resid_true",   ]),
  model = rep(c("Change score", "Residualized (noisy T1)", "Residualized (true T1)"),
              each = n_reps)
)

p1 <- ggplot(pval_df, aes(x = p, fill = model, color = model)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.06, y = 14, vjust = 1.5, hjust = 0,
           label = "α = .05", color = "grey40", size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#2166ac", "#d73027", "#4dac26")) +
  scale_fill_manual( values = c("#2166ac", "#d73027", "#4dac26")) +
  labs(
    x        = "p-value for X",
    y        = "Density",
    color    = NULL, fill = NULL,
    title    = "P-value distributions under the null",
    subtitle = sprintf("SD of noise = %.1f  |  %d reps  |  n = %d", pval_sd, n_reps, n)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.95, 0.95),
        legend.justification = c("right", "top"))

p2 <- pval_df |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(pct_sig = mean(p < 0.05) * 100, .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = pct_sig, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = 9, label = "α = .05",
           color = "grey40", size = 3.5, hjust = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2166ac", "#d73027", "#4dac26")) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) stringr::str_wrap(x, width = 12)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% p < .05", title = "False positive rate") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p1 + p2 + plot_layout(widths = c(3, 3))

Case 3: Monte Carlo simulation across noise (\(\sigma^2\)) levels

To quantify how this bias relates to measurement error, we sweep \(\sigma^2\) (sd_val) from 0 to 2 in steps of .1 and run 1000 replications at each level, extracting the standardized β for X from each model using lm.beta.

\[ \quad \varepsilon_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) \]

Code 
sd_range  <- seq(0, 2, by = 0.1)
set.seed(2026)

beta_rows <- c("change_score.X", "resid_noisy.X", "resid_true.X")
cor_rows  <- c("cor_m1_T1", "cor_m2_T1", "cor_m1_m2", "cor_m1_X", "cor_m2_X")

sim_results <- lapply(sd_range, function(noise_sd) {
  reps <- replicate(n_reps, {
    sim <- as.data.frame(mvrnorm(n, mu = c(0, 0, 0), Sigma = s))
    colnames(sim) <- c("T1", "X", "delta")
    sim$T1_m1  <- sim$T1 + rnorm(n, 0, noise_sd)
    sim$T1_m2  <- sim$T1 + rnorm(n, 0, noise_sd)
    sim$T2     <- sim$T1_m2 + sim$delta
    sim$change <- sim$T2 - sim$T1_m1
    c(
      change_score = lm.beta(lm(change ~ X,      data = sim))["X"],
      resid_noisy  = lm.beta(lm(T2 ~ X + T1_m1, data = sim))["X"],
      resid_true   = lm.beta(lm(T2 ~ X + T1,    data = sim))["X"],
      cor_m1_T1    = cor(sim$T1_m1, sim$T1),
      cor_m2_T1    = cor(sim$T1_m2, sim$T1),
      cor_m1_m2    = cor(sim$T1_m1, sim$T1_m2),
      cor_m1_X     = cor(sim$T1_m1, sim$X),
      cor_m2_X     = cor(sim$T1_m2, sim$X)
    )
  })
  list(
    beta = data.frame(
      sd    = noise_sd,
      model = beta_rows,
      mean  = rowMeans(reps[beta_rows, ]),
      se    = apply(reps[beta_rows, ], 1, function(x) sd(x)) / sqrt(n_reps)
    ),
    cors = data.frame(
      sd   = noise_sd,
      pair = cor_rows,
      mean = rowMeans(reps[cor_rows, ]),
      se   = apply(reps[cor_rows, ], 1, function(x) sd(x)) / sqrt(n_reps)
    )
  )
})

plot_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sim_results, `[[`, "beta"))
plot_df$model <- factor(plot_df$model,
  levels = beta_rows,
  labels = c("Change score", "Residualized (noisy T1)", "Residualized (true T1)"))

cor_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sim_results, `[[`, "cors"))
Code 
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = sd, y = mean, color = model, fill = model)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se),
              alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#2166ac", "#d73027", "#4dac26")) +
  scale_fill_manual( values = c("#2166ac", "#d73027", "#4dac26")) +
  labs(
    x        = "SD of measurement noise",
    y        = "Mean standardized β for X",
    color    = NULL,
    fill     = NULL,
    title    = "Residualized change bias grows with measurement noise",
    subtitle = sprintf("Monte Carlo: %d reps per noise level, n = %d, r(X, T1) = %.1f",
                       n_reps, n, r)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

Takeaway: Residualized change leads to false positives

As measurement noise in the baseline construct increases, the residualized change model drifts away from zero despite there being no true effect. The change score and residualized change with the true (perfectly measured) T1 remain unbiased throughout.

This is the case when:

  1. Your parameter of interest is change
  2. X has a relationship with T1 (this link can be broken through a natural experiment or an RCT)
  3. Imperfect measurement of T1 (essentially all human outcomes)

To have your cake and eat it to the only solution I am aware of is the multiple indicator latent change score model (with strict measurement invariance). For a great tutorial paper (click here)[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6614039/]! With more than two timepoints you can get a better slope estimate using longitudinal mixed effects modeling or latent growth curve modeling (tutorial link).
